Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. For a witnessed-other-trauma presentation, the other threat items describe hypervigilance and startle around other people, and the triggers/memory/appraisal items do not suggest a home-intrusion or boundary-violation danger theme. Repeated door/window checking points to a specific safety behavior focused on securing the environment, which is not supported elsewhere in the selected items and does not fit the formulation well, especially given that maladaptive-strategy links are inactive.

vignette:
Rangi Taufa is a 71-year-old Tongan-American man who has been married for over forty years and works as a cashier at a large grocery store in a suburb of Salt Lake City. He presented for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 57, describing a level of distress that had quietly accumulated over several years before finally becoming, in his own words, "too heavy to carry alone."

Approximately three years ago, Rangi witnessed a violent incident in his neighbourhood in which a young mother and her infant were attacked outside an apartment building. He was standing near the entrance when the assault began - the door swung open with force, the baby began screaming, and the violence unfolded in front of him before anyone could intervene. He called emergency services but felt paralysed, unable to act further. The perpetrator was known to the building's management and, in Rangi's view, had been reported and ignored on multiple prior occasions. No meaningful legal consequences followed. Rangi returned home that night and has not spoken about what he saw in any coherent way since.

What makes Rangi's situation clinically complex is the fractured nature of his memory of the event. He reports feeling as though he is only remembering parts of what happened, with large sections simply absent, and when he attempts to recount it - even to himself - he loses the thread entirely and cannot finish. This absence of a coherent narrative means that rather than processing the event as something contained in the past, Rangi experiences it as perpetually unresolved, and the fragmented quality of his memory keeps him in a state of chronic alertness. When a fragment does surface - the force of the door, the pitch of the infant's cry - it does not arrive as a bounded recollection but as a live signal, and in its wake the sounds and sensations that surrounded the original event become charged once more: a door banging in the store, a baby's wail from the next aisle, a sudden jolt of bodily discomfort all feel, in those moments, indistinguishable from the event itself. He cannot locate the event in time, and so his nervous system treats it as ongoing. When fragments surface, they tend to arrive not as story but as sensation - and those sensations have become tightly bound to specific features of the world around him.

The sound of a baby crying, a door opening or slamming, any sudden feeling of discomfort in his body - these are the threads that pull him back. At the grocery store where he works, these triggers are inescapable. Customers push through the automatic doors with a bang; parents wheel infants past his register; the ambient noise of the store is punctuated constantly by sounds that his nervous system has marked as warnings. Each trigger lands not merely as an unpleasant reminder but as a signal of imminent danger, sending him into a state of heightened alertness in which he scans nearby customers for signs of threat, braces against unexpected movement, and monitors everyone who approaches his lane. His colleagues have noticed that he seems tense and watchful, and one supervisor gently asked whether he was feeling well - a conversation Rangi deflected and has since avoided repeating.

The triggers do more than activate his threat system. They also pull forward the bitterest of his appraisals: that the people who should have protected that mother and child failed to do so, and that no one was ever held accountable. But the relationship runs in the other direction as well: the sheer persistence of the alarm - the way his body floods with danger at the sound of a door, day after day, year after year - has become its own argument. Feeling this afraid, this constantly, has quietly convinced Rangi that the fear must be warranted, that a world capable of producing such unrelenting dread is precisely the kind of world where harm is permitted to continue unchecked and where no one in authority can be trusted to stop it. Each time a door slams and his body floods with alarm, he is not only frightened - he is reminded of that institutional failure, and the anger and helplessness that come with it. He has come to feel, in a way he finds difficult to articulate, that the world is a place where harm is permitted to continue unchecked. This belief in turn feeds his vigilance: if institutions cannot be trusted to prevent violence, then he must watch for it himself. He monitors people closely, reads their movements, and stays on guard - not as a choice but as a compulsion that exhausts him.

The appraisals themselves seem to act as a barrier to memory processing. When Rangi tries to approach what he witnessed, the weight of feeling let down and the absence of any resolution make it feel intolerable to stay with the fragments long enough to form anything coherent. The story remains broken. And the broken story, cycling back, keeps the triggers sharp and the threat system primed.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was his wife's observation that he had become unreachable - present in the house but absent in every way that mattered. He describes feeling dead inside. What he is most afraid of is that this is simply who he is now. What he is hoping, quietly, is that someone can help him find the rest of the story.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that Rangi's sense of threat or heightened alertness causally drives or intensifies his negative appraisals (e.g., that feeling in danger leads him to believe the world is unsafe or that institutions have failed him); the causal direction runs from appraisals to threat throughout, but not the reverse.

Although the vignette states that the fragmented memory keeps triggers 'sharp' in the final paragraph, this is expressed as a cyclical summary rather than a clear causal account of how memory fragments directly activate or produce specific triggers; no paragraph explicitly conveys that the intrusive memory drives or gives rise to the triggering stimuli (sounds, door slams, crying) in a causal sense.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that Rangi's sense of threat or heightened alertness causally drives or intensifies his negative appraisals (e.g., that feeling in danger leads him to believe the world is unsafe or that institutions have failed him); the causal direction runs from appraisals to threat throughout, but not the reverse.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Memory → Triggers: Although the vignette states that the fragmented memory keeps triggers 'sharp' in the final paragraph, this is expressed as a cyclical summary rather than a clear causal account of how memory fragments directly activate or produce specific triggers; no paragraph explicitly conveys that the intrusive memory drives or gives rise to the triggering stimuli (sounds, door slams, crying) in a causal sense.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
